title: LEGO Doctor Doom minifigures compared: 2013 original vs two new 2026 versions
summary: A new comparison from LEGO Fan Media creator just2good lines up the classic 2013 Doctor Doom minifigure against two brand-new versions arriving this September.
bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
LEGO's only Doctor Doom minifigure has been the one from 2013's 76005 Spider-Man: Daily Bugle Showdown, a set that retired in 2015 and has since become pricey on the secondary market. That's about to change, as two new sets featuring Doctor Doom minifigures – 76340 Advent Calendar and 76345 Doctor Doom Bust – are set to release on 1 September 2026.

Creator just2good got early access to all three minifigures and put them side by side. The original 2013 figure has a smaller dark green hood and cape, a lighter shade of green on the torso and legs, and a comic-inspired face print with visible skin tone behind the eyes.

The Advent Calendar version keeps a similar silhouette but switches to a fully light-green colour scheme, adds much more detailed torso and leg printing, uses the newer rubber cape instead of fabric, and drops the visible skin tone for a more sinister look.

The Doctor Doom Bust minifigure is different again, based on the Robert Downey Jr version of the character from Avengers: Doomsday.

## Why it matters
For collectors, this ends a 13-year gap where the only way to get a Doctor Doom minifigure was paying inflated resale prices, reportedly over £60. Having two affordable, current-production options at different price points gives fans genuine choice, whether they want the classic comic look or the newer movie-inspired design.

## What to watch next
Both sets are due out on 1 September 2026 – worth checking official LEGO channels closer to release for confirmed pricing and availability.

title: Two LEGO Ideas Interstellar bookend sets hit 10,000 votes days apart
summary: A second Interstellar-themed bookend project has reached the 10,000-vote milestone on LEGO Ideas, just days after a very similar design achieved the same feat.
bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
A fan-designed LEGO Ideas project called *Interstellar: Tesseract Bookends* has officially reached the required 10,000 supporter votes, qualifying it for consideration in the second LEGO Ideas review of 2026. This comes just days after a near-identical concept, *Interstellar: A Look Back in Time Bookend*, hit the same milestone.

Both builds recreate the film's famous bookcase/tesseract scene as a separable bookend, but with different approaches. The newer set is a bit smaller at just under 600 pieces, and adds diorama touches like the Interstellar logo and a quote piece.

Interestingly, the designer behind this latest project, Minibrick41587, already has three other projects that have hit 10,000 votes in this review round, including Remy the Little Chef, plus Hamilton and Miffy-themed builds.

**Rumour/speculation:** It's not confirmed whether either Interstellar project will become an official set. The LEGO Group is unlikely to release two very similar sets at once, but there is a precedent - 21343 Viking Village - where two overlapping fan projects were merged into a single official set, with both designers credited.

## Why it matters
For LEGO Ideas followers and Interstellar fans, this is a fun example of how the platform can throw up overlapping concepts. It also raises genuine questions about how the LEGO Group might handle judging two similar entries in the same review - something collectors will want to watch closely if they're hoping for an official Interstellar set.

## What to watch next
Keep an eye on the second 2026 LEGO Ideas review results to see whether one, both, or neither Interstellar bookend project is selected - and whether the LEGO Group repeats its Viking Village-style merger approach.

title: LEGO Insiders update lets you redeem multiple rewards in one order
summary: LEGO has simplified its Insiders rewards scheme, letting members add physical rewards straight to their basket and redeem up to three per order instead of placing separate orders each time.
bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
LEGO has confirmed an update to its Insiders rewards programme that makes redeeming physical rewards much simpler. Previously, redeeming points for a physical reward meant generating a code and entering it separately at checkout, with only one reward allowed per order.

Now, physical rewards can be added directly to your basket just like a normal set, with points deducted instead of currency. Members can redeem up to three physical rewards in a single order, rather than needing multiple separate orders as before.

Some rewards will still have individual limits, but this change removes the need to place several orders just to grab a couple of items, such as pairing a smaller reward with a poster or similar extra. Non-physical rewards and sweepstakes are unaffected and still use the old code-based redemption method, so any codes you're holding onto can still be used as normal. LEGO says the update is already live on LEGO.com.

## Why it matters
For UK collectors who regularly stack up Insiders points, this is a genuinely useful quality-of-life change. It cuts down on postage costs from multiple deliveries, saves time at checkout, and makes it easier to combine smaller rewards into one tidy order alongside a normal LEGO purchase.

## What to watch next
Worth keeping an eye on whether individual reward limits change over time, and whether LEGO expands this basket-based system to cover sweepstakes or digital rewards in future updates.

What's notable is what's missing: unlike story-driven predecessors such as Hidden Side and Monster Fighters, there are no named characters or explained plot. LEGO's own product page keeps things deliberately vague, describing the Midnight Valley Collection as featuring 'distorted and asymmetrical constructions' that 'create a haunting atmosphere', aimed at fans of mystery and suspense rather than a set storyline.

The reviewer says this ambiguity is intentional and enjoyable, comparing it to classic LEGO Castle sets from years past, where minimal lore left plenty of room for kids' (and now adults') own imagination.

## Why it matters
For UK fans and collectors, this signals a shift in how LEGO Icons approaches its adult-targeted seasonal collections - leaning on atmosphere and building experience rather than spelled-out narratives. If Midnight Valley follows the Winter Village model, it could become a recurring annual release worth watching for future additions and possible expansion sets.

## What to watch next
